title: Chapter 64: Soft 2
content:
Chapter 64

Wei Wuxian drew his flute and played through the notes on the page. Sure enough, the melody fractured right down the middle—the half-phrase concluding the previous page and the fragment starting the next didn't belong to the same piece at all.

There should have been a page sandwiched right between them, meticulously torn out without leaving a trace.

Whoever did it had been surgical; no jagged stub remained, making the theft virtually imperceptible unless you knew the score by heart. Flipping the tome over, Wei Wuxian traced three characters brushed across the deep indigo cover.

"Collection of Turmoil?" Wei Wuxian asked. "What kind of book is this? The melodies inside sound distinctly bizarre."

"A compendium of esoteric scores from the Eastern Seas," Lan Wangji replied.

"From the Eastern Seas? No wonder the cadence feels foreign compared to ours."

Lan Xichen's expression turned grim. "...TheCollection of Turmoil. Legend has it that a cultivator of the Gusu Lan Sect was cast adrift across the sea, wandering those distant eastern shores for years and compiling a volume of sinister melodies. If played while channeling spiritual energy, every score within can be wielded as an instrument of malice—causing chronic wasting, relentless agitation, violent turmoil of the blood, or the gradual loss of the five senses... In the hands of a master, it can snuff out a life within seven notes."

Wei Wuxian smacked the desk. "That's it!"

Caught up in the rush, his strike nearly sent the delicate paper lantern tumbling off the wood. Lan Wangji’s hand shot out, steadying the frame before it hit the floorboards. Wei Wuxian leaned forward: "Lan-zongzhu, is there a song in thisCollection of Turmoilthat unsettles the mind, agitates the spiritual core, sends the blood boiling, and provokes uncontrollable rage?"

Lan Xichen murmured, "...There should be."

"Jin Guangyao lacks the raw spiritual power to strike someone dead in seven beats," Wei Wuxian reasoned. "Besides, killing someone that fast is far too loud—he’d never pick an overt lethal piece. But what if he cloaked it under the guise of playing the Song of Clarity to soothe Chifeng-zun's nerves? If he played it day in and day out for three straight months, could that melody act like a slow-acting poison, steadily accelerating Chifeng-zun’s qi deviation?"

Lan Xichen closed his eyes. "...Yes."

"Then the puzzle pieces fit," Wei Wuxian said. "That rogue passage grafted intoCleansingcame straight from the missing page of this very book. The eastern dark arts recorded here are notoriously intricate, and he didn't have the luxury of time to copy it down in the forbidden chamber, so he tore the page out—no, wait. That's not it. Jin Guangyao has a photographic memory; he didn't rip it out because he couldn't memorize it. He did it to burn the bridge behind him. He needed to ensure that even if the plot blew up in his face or someone caught him red-handed, no one could ever trace the melody back to its source.

"He played every card with surgical caution. In front of you, he brazenly performed the immaculate, untouched version ofCleansing. Chifeng-zun was a warrior, not an artistic connoisseur; he’d heard you playCleansingbefore, so he had a rough memory of the melody. Jin Guangyao wouldn't dare play an overtly sinister tune in front of him. Instead, he went to extraordinary lengths to splice two pieces of radically different styles and polar opposite effects together—and somehow stitched them so seamlessly that they flowed without a hitch. His musical instinct really is terrifying. My guess is that he channeled negligible spiritual energy during the passages ofCleansing, only pouring his core into the segments borrowed from theCollection of Turmoil. Chifeng-zun was no expert in the musical path; how could he ever tell that a portion of his soothing hymn had been perverted into a death knell?"

After a heavy pause, Lan Xichen spoke in a hollow murmur. "...Though he visited the Cloud Recesses often, I never once told him of the forbidden chamber beneath the Library Pavilion."

"Lan-zongzhu, forgive my bluntness," Wei Wuxian countered, "but during the Sunshot Campaign, Lianfang-zun operated deep undercover inside Nightless City itself—and he was an extraordinarily successful spy. He managed to locate Wen Ruohan's private vault, slip in and out without raising an eyebrow, memorize every military map and dossier, and transcribe the intelligence stroke for stroke back to Koi Tower. Compared to that, the hidden room under the Lan Clan's library... wouldn't pose much of a challenge."

Lan Xichen stared down at the transcribed fragment in his hands. "I... must find a way to test this melody."

Lan Wangji looked up sharply. "Brother?"

"When Da-ge passed away, the siege of the Burial Mounds was already over, and Young Master Wei was no longer among the living," Lan Xichen said, his voice straining. "If testing confirms that this melody genuinely unravels the mind and is no mere fabrication, then I..."

"Ze-wu-jun," Wei Wuxian cautioned, "testing a cursed tune on a living soul directly violates the precepts of the Gusu Lan Clan."

"I will test it on myself."

For the leader of Gusu Lan to utter something so completely reckless proved his mind was in absolute turmoil. Lan Wangji’s voice rose with an edge of alarm: "Brother!"

Lan Xichen pressed a hand against his forehead, struggling to hold back the floodgates. "Wangji! The Jin Guangyao I know, the Jin Guangyao you two see, and the Jin Guangyao the world perceives are entirely different people! All these years, in my eyes, he has always been... a man bearing humiliation for the greater good, caring for the common people, deferent to his elders, and gentle to his subordinates. I firmly believed the world's slander was born of prejudice, and that the man I knew was the real him. You expect me to accept in an instant that everything he showed me was a lie? That he orchestrated the murder of his own sworn brother, that I was a pawn in his scheme, and that I unwittingly handed him the knife...? Can you at least allow me to exercise caution before passing judgment?"

Lan Xichen had only ever wanted to bridge the rift between Nie Mingjue and Jin Guangyao. He had taught Jin GuangyaoCleansingout of pure earnestness, entrusting him to soothe Nie Mingjue's spiraling core on his behalf. How was a man supposed to endure the realization that his gentlest intentions had been weaponized into lethal venom?

A suffocating quiet fell over the three of them. Only when they emerged from the Library Pavilion into the cool night air did Lan Wangji break the silence: "I will go see Uncle."

Lan Xichen, who had remained lost in thought, nodded softly. "I will escort Young Master Wei back. Join us once you have finished."

He guided Wei Wuxian along the white stone paths winding through Cloud Recesses, arriving back before that secluded cottage shrouded in gentians. Standing by the porch, Wei Wuxian asked hesitantly, "Does Teacher Lan know about what Hanguang-jun did at Koi Tower...?"

"Uncle woke only recently," Lan Xichen replied. "I instructed everyone to keep silent in his presence."

If Lan Qiren learned about the circus Lan Wangji had pulled alongside the Yiling Laozu at Koi Tower, the poor man would blow a gasket and pass right back out. Wei Wuxian cleared his throat. "Old Master Lan really has his hands full."

"He carries a heavy burden indeed."

Suddenly, Lan Xichen looked toward the quiet building. "Young Master Wei, do you know what place this is?"

"Why would Ze-wu-jun assume I'd know?"

Lan Xichen met his gaze. "This was where my mother resided during her years in Cloud Recesses."

Lan Xichen and Lan Wangji’s mother. Wei Wuxian felt a prickle of confusion. The formal residence of the Gusu Lan Clan Leader had always been the Hanshi, certainly not this humble cottage tucked into an isolated corner. Could Lan Wangji’s parents have been like Jiang Fengmian and Madam Yu—incompatible in temper, forced into marriage, and living estranged under separate roofs?

A sect leader living apart from his formal wife rarely pointed to a cheerful history. Rumors held that Qingheng-jun’s wife had been chronically frail, convalescing year-round behind closed doors, unfit for public company. The outside world knew next to nothing about her; people gossiped that the "illness" was some unspeakable secret, like severe disfigurement or a crippling deformity. Wei Wuxian held his tongue, waiting for Lan Xichen to speak.

"Young Master Wei," Lan Xichen said quietly, "you must know that my father spent decades in seclusion, detached from worldly affairs. For as long as I can remember, the clan was run almost entirely by my uncle."

"I know that much."

Lan Xichen let his hands fall, Liebing disappearing into the folds of his white sleeve. "My father's lifelong seclusion was entirely because of my mother. To call this her residence... would be generous. It was a place of house arrest."

Wei Wuxian stopped in his tracks.

Qingheng-jun, the father of the Twin Jades, had once been a legendary figure in his own right. Renowned in his youth and basking in peerless glory, he had abruptly retired at the cusp of coming of age, announcing a sudden marriage and withdrawing entirely from the world. Though framed as cultivation in seclusion, it had looked far more like complete hermitage. Many had guessed at the truth, but no one had ever verified it.

Lan Xichen knelt beside the patch of gentians, his fingers gently brushing the delicate violet petals. "When my father was young, on his journey back from a night-hunt, he encountered my mother outside Gusu." He offered a faint, melancholy smile. "They said it was love at first sight."

Wei Wuxian smiled faintly. "Youth is always romantic."

"Yet she held no love for him," Lan Xichen continued. "And she had killed one of my father’s dearest mentors."

The revelation hit like a thunderbolt. Knowing it was improper to pry into family scandals, but thinking of Lan Wangji, Wei Wuxian couldn't help himself. "Why?!"

"I do not know," Lan Xichen murmured. "Though in this world, it rarely strays beyond the web of grievance and vengeance."

Wei Wuxian held back his questions. "And... what happened next?"

"Then," Lan Xichen said, "learning the truth tore my father apart. Yet after agonizing turmoil, he brought her back to Gusu in secret. Defying the elders' outrage, he quietly bowed before heaven and earth with her in marriage, telling the entire clan: she is my wife for this life and the next. If anyone wishes to lay a hand on her, they must go through me first."

Wei Wuxian’s eyes went wide.

"Once the rites were concluded," Lan Xichen continued, "my father arranged a cottage to lock my mother away, and chose another to seal himself inside. In name, it was secluded cultivation; in reality, it was self-imposed penance."

He paused. "Young Master Wei, do you understand why he chose that path?"

Wei Wuxian fell silent for a long moment before answering softly, "He couldn't forgive the killer of his beloved master, yet he couldn't bear to watch the woman he loved be put to death. His only compromise was to marry her to shield her life, while forcing himself never to lay eyes on her again."

"Do you believe he was in the right?"

"I don't know."

Lan Xichen looked faintly lost. "Then what would have been right?"

"I don't know."

Lan Xichen whispered, "My father cast everything to the wind. The clan elders were incandescent with rage, but having watched him grow up, their hands were tied. All they could do was guard the secret fiercely, dropping hints to the outside world that the sect leader's wife suffered from a delicate illness that prevented her from receiving guests. The moment Wangji and I were born, we were whisked away to be raised by wet nurses. Once we grew a little older, our education was handed entirely to our uncle.

"My uncle was an unbending, righteous man by nature. Seeing my mother’s actions ruin my father's life made him despise moral deviance above all else. He drilled Wangji and me with unforgiving strictness, pouring every ounce of discipline into us. We were permitted to see our mother only once a month, right here in this cottage."

Two young boys, facing only a severe uncle, relentless expectations, and towering stacks of texts day in and day out. No matter how exhausted they were, they had to keep their spines straight, striving to be the clan's brightest prodigies and everyone's shining paragon. Deprived of their parents, unable to roughhouse in their father's arms or curl up against their mother's chest.

And through it all, they had done nothing wrong.

"Whenever Wangji and I came to visit," Lan Xichen said, "she never once complained about being cooped up here, nor did she ever quiz us on our studies. She loved teasing Wangji most of all. But the more she teased, the quieter he became, his little face turning so sour—he was like that even as a toddler. Still," a soft smile curled his lips, "though Wangji never said a word, I knew he counted down the days to see her every month. He did, and so did I."

Wei Wuxian pictured a pint-sized Lan Wangji scooped up in his mother's embrace, his pale cheeks flushed pink with childish indignation, and couldn't help smiling along. But before the warmth could settle, Lan Xichen spoke again:

"Then one day, Uncle suddenly told us: we didn't need to go anymore.

"Mother was gone."

Wei Wuxian asked softly, "How old was Lan Zhan?"

"Six."

"He was too young to grasp what 'gone' truly meant. No matter how the servants coaxed or how fiercely Uncle scolded, he kept coming here every single month, sitting quietly under the veranda, waiting for someone to open that door. Later, as he grew older and understood that she was never coming back and that no one would ever open it again... he still came."

Lan Xichen rose to his feet, his dark eyes meeting Wei Wuxian’s. "Wangji has always been stubborn to a fault."

The night breeze rustled the canopy overhead, setting the sea of gentians swaying in waves of deep violet. Wei Wuxian’s gaze drifted toward the wooden porch, almost picturing a tiny child wearing a neat forehead ribbon, sitting rigidly on the planks, waiting in stubborn silence for a door that would never open.

"Madam Lan must have been a very gentle woman," he said softly.

"In my memories, she truly was," Lan Xichen replied. "I never knew why she did what she did, and in truth..." He took a slow breath, confessing quietly, "...I never wanted to know."

After a quiet pause, Lan Xichen lowered his eyes and lifted Liebing. The night wind carried a low, weeping breath of music, drifting into the dark like an aching sigh.

Wei Wuxian had heard Lan Xichen play Liebing before; his music had always mirrored Ze-wu-jun himself—warm as a spring rain, gentle and luminous. But tonight, though the mastery remained peerless, the melody tasted of pure bitterness.

The mountain breeze ruffled Lan Xichen’s dark hair and tilted his forehead ribbon, yet the clan leader, usually so fastidious about decorum, paid it no mind. Only when the final note faded into the trees did he lower Liebing. "Music is strictly forbidden late at night in Cloud Recesses. I have broken rule after rule tonight—pardon the spectacle, Young Master Wei."

Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Think nothing of it. Has Ze-wu-jun forgotten? The man standing in front of you holds the reigning record for breaking rules here..."

Lan Xichen gave a rueful smile. "My brother's and my origins have never been whispered to outsiders; I had no business sharing them with you. Tonight, I simply found myself desperate to confide in someone. A moment of impulse."

"I'm not one to flap my jaws," Wei Wuxian assured him. "Ze-wu-jun can rest easy."

"Though I suspect Wangji would never hide anything from you anyway."

"If he doesn't want to talk about it, I won't pry."

"Given Wangji's nature, if you don't pry, how could he ever bring himself to speak? And even if you do ask, there are truths he would still keep buried."

Wei Wuxian opened his mouth to reply, but footsteps rustled along the path behind them. Turning around, Lan Wangji strode through the pale moonlight. Dangling from his right hand were two plump clay jars sealed in brilliant scarlet wax.

Wei Wuxian’s eyes lit up. "Hanguang-jun, aren't you a sweetheart!"
